p: Yashwant Rao was the third son of Tukoji Rao Holkar. He was educated in accountancy and could read Persian, Marathi and Urdu. On 29 January 1797 Tukoji named his eldest son, Kashi Rao, as his successor. The second son, Malhar Rao, rebelled and Yashwant Rao joined him; on 14 September the army of Daulat Rao Scindia surprised their camp, Malhar Rao was killed and Yashwant Rao fled wounded. He gathered a following that included Pindharis and Afghans under Mir Khan. Claiming to act for his infant nephew Khande Rao, he declared himself head of the Holkars in January 1799, and by April had defeated Kashi Rao's commander, the Chevalier Dudrenec.

In 1799 the widows of Mahadaji Scindia asked his help to recover Ujjain and promised him four lakh rupees; he accepted five lakh from Ambaji Ingle to betray them, and looted the city. His victory over Scindia and the Peshwa on 25 October 1802, the day of Diwali, was won at Hadapsar near Pune. The Peshwa fled to Sinhagad, and Holkar took over the administration at Pune and appointed Amrutrao as Peshwa. The British, fearing for their own territories and those of their ally the Nizam of Hyderabad, decided to restore the Peshwa under their protection.

On 8 October 1804 he marched on Delhi to gain control of the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II and besieged it for more than a week, but could not overcome the defence under Colonel Ochterlony. The emperor nevertheless gave him the title Maharajadhiraja Raj Rajeshwar Alija Bahadur. He appealed to other Indian rulers to join him against the British, but Daulat Rao Scindia would not fight and others gave no direct help. He fled to the Sikh Empire, where Ranjit Singh refused a British request to arrest him.

By the treaty signed at Rajghat on 24 December 1805 the British returned his territory, accepted his dominion over Jaipur, Udaipur, Kota and Bundi and undertook not to interfere in Holkar affairs; he gave up his claims to Bundelkhand and the lands north of the Chambal. He thus avoided the subsidiary alliance imposed on other Maratha chiefs. Lord Lake resigned in protest at the abandonment of the Company's Indian allies. In a letter of 15 February 1806 Holkar wrote that he had concluded the war when he found himself abandoned on all sides. He died on 28 October 1811.

notes: The 'Battles' section of the saved article is nearly empty (a table lost?), so Monson's retreat, which the entry names, and the siege of Bharatpur could not be told.
The article is strongly admiring ('one of the foremost generals in Indian history'); I kept to events. The Ujjain betrayal is from the article.
The article uses Sindhia, Shinde and Scindia for the same house; I used Scindia.
The article calls the entry's 'ruler of Indore from 1799' 'Raja of Indore State' and dates his self-declaration to January 1799.
